title: Shimon and the worth of silence
carry: nothing better than silence, said the sage

segments.voice: Yesterday's word: menuchat hanefesh, calm of soul, the jar that clears when you set it down. Today, a new week and a trait made of saying less. You met this sage's line on day two hundred forty-seven; now it becomes a practice.

The group chat has been going all morning. Opinions, jokes, a small argument, someone apologizing for the argument, someone else restarting it. Then one person who hasn't said anything all day types a single sentence, and everyone stops. Why does that one land? Partly because it's good. Partly because it came out of quiet. Words from someone who speaks all the time blur together. Words from someone who keeps silence get weighed.
screen: `THE CHAT HASN'T STOPPED.` → `ONE SENTENCE FROM THE QUIET ONE.` → `WORDS FROM SILENCE GET WEIGHED.`

segments.voice: Shtikah. Silence. Four angles. First, the sage. In Pirkei Avot, Shimon, the son of Rabban Gamliel, says that all his days he grew up among the sages, and found nothing better for the body than silence. Then he adds two lines: what matters most is not study but doing, and whoever multiplies words brings on sin. Raised among learned voices, he came away with the value of the closed mouth. Second, Proverbs. Even a fool, when he holds his peace, is counted wise, and one who shuts his lips is thought to have understanding. Half a joke, half a warning: fewer words leave fewer chances to show what you don't know, and fewer chances to hurt someone. Third, the practice. Some Jews keep what's called a taanit dibbur, a fast from speech: a set stretch of hours with no talking at all, sometimes in a season of repentance. Some Mussar teachers recommend smaller versions, an hour, a meal, a commute, as a way of feeling how much of what people say is filler, or heat, or a reach to be seen. Fourth, the measure. Like every trait in this block, silence has a right amount. Remember the two pockets from humility day: there are moments when staying quiet is a failure, when someone is being wronged or a truth needs saying. Shtikah isn't swallowing what matters. It's clearing away what doesn't, so that what matters can be heard.
screen: `NOTHING BETTER THAN SILENCE.` · `EVEN A FOOL IS COUNTED WISE.` · `A FAST FROM SPEECH.` · `NOT SWALLOWING WHAT MATTERS.` · then, large: `SILENCE.`

segments.voice: Close your mouth gently and let your tongue rest. Notice the words that still rise, things to say, replies to rehearse, a comment for later, and don't stop them; just watch them come and go, unspoken. If you pray, let the silence itself be a kind of listening; if not, simply let it be quiet.
Shtikah. Silence: guarding speech by speaking less, so the words that do come out are worth weighing. Today's word.
Your line: nothing better than silence, said the sage. Words that come out of quiet can be fewer, kinder and more true. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Some Jews keep a taanit dibbur, a set stretch of time with no speech, and in Mussar practice people working on shtikah set themselves shorter periods of silence, such as an hour or a meal.
